subject: business-studies
title: Break-Even: Where Revenue Catches Total Cost

slides.heading: Break-Even: Where Revenue Catches Total Cost
bullets: How fixed costs of $2,000 stay flat, total cost rises from $2,000 by $10 per unit, and revenue rising at $20 per unit catches it at 200 units
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build a break-even chart line by line, from flat fixed costs to the single crossing where revenue catches total cost.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Describe break-even in order: flat fixed costs, total cost from the $2,000 intercept, revenue rising faster, the crossing at 200 units
Explain why the business makes a loss below 200 units and a profit above 200 units
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud and tell the class: by the end you will be able to read any break-even chart and state the break-even output and revenue.

slides.heading: Selling more - but when does the business stop losing money?
bullets: Fixed costs are $2,000 even if nothing is made or sold
Each unit costs $10 in variable costs and sells for $20, so how many units must be sold to cover all costs?
slides.notes: Ask the class: if every sale brings in more than its variable cost, why is there still a loss at low output? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the fixed costs must be covered first.

slides.heading: Break-even is where total revenue equals total cost
bullets: Fixed costs stay at $2,000 at every output, while variable costs rise by $10 for each extra unit
Total cost starts at $2,000 and rises by $10 per unit; total revenue starts at zero and rises faster, by $20 per unit
The two lines cross once, at 200 units, where revenue and total cost are both $4,000
slides.notes: Stress the deciding idea: total cost does not start at zero - it starts at fixed costs - and revenue rises faster, so there is exactly one break-even point.

slides.heading: Axes first, then the flat fixed-cost line
bullets: Rent and insurance cost $2,000 however much the business makes, so the fixed-cost line is flat at $2,000
Output rises along the horizontal axis, but the fixed-cost line never leaves $2,000
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and point to the flat line: sweep across the outputs and show the fixed-cost value staying at $2,000 at every output.

slides.heading: Total cost starts at fixed costs, then rises
bullets: At zero output total cost is already $2,000, because fixed costs must still be paid
Each extra unit adds $10 of variable cost, so total cost rises steadily from the $2,000 intercept
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and start at the intercept: total cost begins at $2,000, not zero, then climbs by $10 for each unit.

slides.heading: Revenue rises faster, but still in loss
bullets: Total revenue starts at zero and rises by $20 for each unit sold, faster than total cost
Below 200 units total cost is still above revenue, so the business is in the loss zone
slides.notes: Play scene 3 and compare the slopes: revenue at $20 per unit is steeper than total cost at $10 per unit, so the gap closes - but has not closed yet.

slides.heading: Break-even, then the profit zone opens
bullets: At 200 units revenue and total cost both equal $4,000 - this is the break-even point
Above 200 units revenue is above total cost, so the profit zone opens; below it is the loss zone
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and mark the crossing: 200 units and $4,000, with loss on the left of the point and profit on the right.

slides.heading: Worked example: finding the 200-unit break-even
bullets: Contribution per unit is $20 selling price minus $10 variable cost, which is $10 per unit
Break-even output is $2,000 fixed costs divided by $10 contribution, which is 200 units, giving break-even revenue of $4,000
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, fixed costs $2,000. Step 2, contribution $10 per unit. Step 3, $2,000 divided by $10 is 200 units. Step 4, 200 units at $20 is $4,000 of revenue, exactly covering total cost.

slides.heading: Your turn: read the chart
bullets: In pairs: state total cost and total revenue at 100 units and at 300 units, and say whether each is a loss or a profit
Then swap and check: did your partner start total cost at $2,000, instead of at zero?
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for intercept reasoning, then take two pairs answers: at 100 units a loss, at 300 units a profit, crossing at 200 units.

slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who says total cost starts at zero like revenue
Name the $2,000 intercept, the $10 and $20 slopes, and the 200-unit crossing to earn full credit
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers follow both lines from their starting points to the single crossing.
